answers.ma_evidence:
- Statement I is false. Continuity does not imply differentiability. For example, the function $y=|x-1|$ is continuous but it's not differentiable at $x=1.$

- Statement II is true.  A function that is discontinuous at a point can't be differentiable at this point (because differentiability implies continuity).

- Statement III is true. Indeed, differentiability implies continuity.

- Statement I is false and statement III is true. Indeed,  let's investigate the continuity of $f(x).$ It is continuous everywhere except, possibly, $x=1.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}(-x+4)=-1+4=3 \\ {lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(x+2)=1+2=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)\ne f(1)=0,
$$

and so $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=1$ (it has a removable discontinuity there). Hence, it is also not differentiable at this point.

- Statement II is false. Since $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=1,$ it is not differentiable on any interval containing this point. Consequently, it is not differentiable on $(-2,2).$
